prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
SubagentHandback({message: "Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and they should teach it with more purpose than many of them do now, because the strongest arguments for abandoning it rest on a picture of the classroom that the evidence about how children learn does not support. The case against cursive is easy to state and sounds modern: children will spend their adult lives typing and swiping, the hours given to practising loops and joins could go to coding or reading or maths, and a skill that most adults abandon within a few years of leaving school is a poor use of scarce lessons. Finland dropped compulsory cursive in 2016, a number of American states have gone back and forth on it, and any teacher who has watched a nine-year-old grind through a page of looped letters while the clock runs down will feel the pull of that argument. Yet it treats handwriting as a delivery mechanism for words that could just as well arrive by another route, when for a young child it is also one of the main ways the words are learned in the first place.

The most persuasive research here concerns what happens in the brain when children form letters by hand compared with when they press keys. Karin James and her colleagues at Indiana University scanned pre-literate children after they had either drawn letters freehand, traced them, or typed them, and found that only the drawn letters produced strong activity in the regions of the brain that later support reading. An earlier French study by Marieke Longcamp found a similar pattern, and a 2024 Norwegian study using EEG reported richer patterns of connectivity between brain regions when students wrote by hand than when they typed. None of this proves that joined writing in particular is the active ingredient, and anyone who claims otherwise is overreaching, but it does establish that the slow, variable, effortful business of making a letter with a pen leaves a more useful trace than selecting one from a keyboard, where every A is the same press of the same key whatever the child understands about its shape. If handwriting matters for learning to read and spell, then the question for a school is how to teach it well, and the choice between print and joined script is a question about method inside that larger commitment.

Here an honest advocate has to concede something. The research does not show that cursive beats print as a route to literacy, and some of the claims made for it in newspaper columns, that it unlocks a special kind of thinking or that it is the cure for poor spelling, go well beyond what anyone has measured. The defensible claim is narrower and still sufficient. Handwriting that is fluent and automatic frees a child's attention for composition, which is why Steve Graham and other researchers on writing development have found repeatedly that children who write more easily tend to write longer, more developed texts. A child still forming each letter as a separate act is spending working memory on the pen that she needs for the sentence, and joined writing is the natural way to remove that cost, since it lets the hand move through a word as a single gesture rather than lifting and repositioning after every letter. The same motor logic is part of why children who learn to join letters often become better at spelling common sequences such as the ending of a verb or the vowel pair in a familiar word, because the hand remembers a pattern the eye might skim past.

Speed deserves more weight than it usually gets in the debate. By the later years of primary school, and certainly by secondary school, pupils are expected to write for extended periods, in examinations, in note-taking, in the daily work of every subject, and the ones who cannot do it quickly and legibly are penalised in ways that have nothing to do with their understanding. Printed writing, with its lifted pen and its separated letters, tops out at a slower pace than a fluent joined hand, and the pupils who go on printing into their teens tend to hit that ceiling at exactly the moment the demands on them rise. Teaching joins at seven or eight, when the motor habits are still forming, is far easier than trying to rebuild a hand at fourteen when a child has already settled into an idiosyncratic and inefficient way of forming letters that no one corrected. The sensible time to give a child a handwriting that will survive pressure is during the years when she is still receptive to being taught one.

The objection that children will type anyway answers a different question from the one a primary school faces. Nobody is proposing that typing be banned; the point is that typing and handwriting do different jobs, and the reasoning from tomorrow's tools to today's curriculum gets the order wrong. A child can learn to touch-type in a matter of weeks at eleven or twelve, once the rest of literacy is secure, whereas the benefits of early handwriting come from doing it at the age when letters are still being learned. It is also worth noticing that the national tests and most public examinations in England and many other countries still require extended handwritten answers, so a school that stopped teaching a fluent hand would be sending pupils into high-stakes situations without the skill those situations demand, and the pupils who would suffer most are the ones whose families cannot supply the extra tuition or the typing practice at home that would paper over the gap.

That last point carries a fairness argument that tends to be missed by people who treat handwriting as a relic. Children from comfortable homes will acquire keyboards, tablets, and the habit of using them regardless of what the school does, and many of them will also be handed pens, notebooks, and patient adults who sit beside them practising letters. Children without those advantages depend on the school to teach the skills that the school will later test, and handwriting is one of the cheapest to teach and one of the most visible when it is missing. Dropping it from the curriculum in the name of modernity would widen an existing gap, because the pupils who most need a systematic, taught approach would be the ones left to pick it up, or not, by chance.

Children with particular difficulties are sometimes cited on the other side, and the case deserves a careful answer rather than a dismissal. Some pupils with dysgraphia or motor-coordination problems find joined writing painful, and for them a keyboard is a legitimate and often transformative accommodation, which any good school should provide without fuss. Yet the existence of children for whom an alternative is necessary does not show that the default should be abolished for everyone, any more than the existence of children who need hearing aids shows that the school should stop speaking. There is in fact some evidence and a good deal of classroom experience suggesting that joined writing can help children with dyslexia, because starting each letter from the baseline with an entry stroke makes the common confusions between b and d, or p and q, harder to produce, since the joins give each letter a direction of travel that the printed form lacks. Evidence of this kind is thinner than anyone would like, and a school should watch what works for each child rather than apply a rule, but it points toward flexibility within a taught approach rather than away from teaching one.

What the sceptics are right about is that a lot of cursive teaching has been bad. Children have been made to copy elaborate looped capitals that no adult uses, to spend months on exercises in slanted ovals, and to be marked down for individuality in how a letter is shaped, when the point of the exercise is a hand that is legible and quick rather than a replica of a copybook from 1950. The better schemes now in use begin joining early, use simple forms with few loops, introduce the joins in families so that children learn them as patterns rather than as isolated shapes, and accept that a mature hand will drift from the model in ways that are perfectly fine provided it stays readable. This is a more modest and more useful skill than the one parents remember, and it can be taught in short daily sessions that take a fraction of the time previous generations devoted to it, leaving the hours the sceptics want for other subjects largely intact. If the argument against cursive is really an argument against the old way of teaching it, then it deserves to win, and it wins by improving the lessons rather than by removing them.

There is also something to be said for the less quantifiable matters that tend to get a sentimental hearing and then be set aside. A great deal of the written record of every family, every town, and every country is in handwriting, much of it joined, and a child who cannot read it is cut off from letters, diaries, parish registers, and the marginal notes of her own grandparents in a way that no scanning project fully repairs. Being able to read cursive is a smaller thing than being able to write it, and it could in theory be taught separately, but in practice the two tend to travel together, since the surest way to read a script is to have formed its letters yourself. A signature, whatever else is said about its place in a digital world, is still how people mark a document as their own, and a child who has never developed a settled hand has nothing to sign with except a few stiffly printed capitals.

None of this requires pretending that handwriting is the centrepiece of the primary curriculum, or that a child who writes in print is doomed. It requires only that we weigh what a small amount of well-taught practice buys against what its absence would cost, and the balance falls clearly on one side: the research on early letter learning favours the pen, the demands of later schooling reward a fast and legible hand, the fairness considerations favour teaching what will be tested, and the accommodations that children with difficulties need are easily made without abandoning the rule. Primary schools should therefore go on teaching joined-up handwriting, beginning early, using plain and practical letterforms, keeping the sessions short and regular, and treating a keyboard as a second skill added in later years rather than as a replacement for the first one. A child who leaves primary school able to write fluently by hand and to type competently has two tools where the alternative offers one, and giving every child both costs very little and takes nothing away from the rest of what a school is for."})
